messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Vignette:
Asha, a 30-year-old South Asian software engineer, came to therapy after years of living with a tightly managed sense that danger could appear without warning. She grew up in a home where her caregiver’s physical abuse was a private family reality that never felt named or escaped, only endured. In later recollections, Asha could describe fragments with striking precision—the taste in her mouth during certain episodes, the sharp smell of sweat on skin when she was being grabbed or cornered, the heavy, sour smell of alcohol on his breath when his mood turned and she knew something was wrong—but the memories never came to her in a clean sequence. When she tried to tell what had happened, she would stop midway, saying she could not put the pieces in order. Some parts felt vivid and immediate, while others seemed to vanish just as she reached them, as if her mind pushed them away before she could fully see them. What stayed with her most was not a single image but a scattered, bodily sense of being trapped with an adult whose anger could become physical at any moment.

As a child, Asha learned to track the smallest details of threat. The smell of alcohol in the house signaled that she needed to be careful, and the combination of sweat and body odour on an adult who had already begun to loom over her made her stomach tighten before anything had even happened. She remembered that one particular taste—something specific to those moments—would rise in her mouth and make her feel ill, and even now she could not always say when that taste first entered the memory because the memory itself arrived incomplete. In the years after the abuse, these sensory traces did not stay in the past. They began appearing unexpectedly in ordinary adult settings, making her feel suddenly flooded and then ashamed of how quickly she had to pull away from whatever she was doing. She was not describing flashbacks in technical terms; instead, she said that when the memory came, it came too much. The feeling would crest so quickly that she had to stop talking, stop thinking, sometimes leave the room, because the emotion seemed larger than her ability to hold it.

By the time she was married and working as a software engineer, Asha had developed a life that looked steady from the outside but was organized around being ready. At home she repeatedly checked that the doors and windows were locked, often more than once before bed, and she found it hard to let herself relax even when she knew she was safe in her apartment with her husband. She could recognize the irrationality of it, but the knowledge did not settle her body. Nights were especially difficult; she had trouble falling asleep and would wake up alert, scanning the apartment and mentally revisiting whether she had locked everything properly. In the morning she was often tired before her day started, but she still moved through the routines of work, careful not to let colleagues see how much effort it took to keep herself composed.

The workplace itself became one of the places where her symptoms were quietly encountered. In the open-plan office and during team meetings, she sometimes caught a whiff of alcohol from a coworker returning from lunch, or body odour from someone standing too close in a conference room, and the sensation would pull her abruptly inward. She would sit a little straighter, focus on the laptop screen, and wait for the wave of discomfort to pass. At home, if a bottle of alcohol had been opened at a social gathering, the smell would remain in her mind long after the guests left, and she would find herself checking locks again before settling for the night. Over time she began declining some invitations, not because she wanted to isolate herself, but because she could not predict when a smell or taste would catch her off guard and leave her struggling to recover her composure. Her husband noticed that she stayed tense even on quiet evenings, as though rest itself required permission she could not quite give.

What finally brought Asha to seek help was the combination of exhaustion and fear that her life had become narrower than she wanted to admit. She was tired of sleeping lightly, tired of the repeated checking, and tired of feeling overwhelmed by fragments of memory that arrived uninvited and then slipped away before she could make sense of them. She said she wanted to understand why certain smells and tastes could still reach her so quickly, and why her body seemed to remain on guard even in places she knew were secure. Most of all, she was afraid that if she kept pushing the memories away, they would continue to hover at the edge of her life indefinitely; at the same time, she hoped that treatment might help her face them in a way that did not leave her flooded and unable to continue.
